Occupational Lung Disease

matching occupational exposure to lung disease · upper vs lower lobes · pleural plaques · cancer and tuberculosis riskWhat did the patient breathe at work, which lobes are involved, and is the pleura involved?

1Illness script
Bottom line
  • The job names the dust the lobes and the pleura confirm it: asbestos at the bases with pleural plaques; silica, coal and beryllium at the apices
  • Asbestos bronchogenic carcinoma far more than mesothelioma; smoking multiplies only the carcinoma
  • Silicosis tuberculosis risk, a yearly tuberculin test; berylliosis granulomas like sarcoidosis
What it is

Lung fibrosis from a mineral dust inhaled at work; hypersensitivity pneumonitis is the organic-antigen look-alike

Driver

Years of exposure dust-laden macrophages inflammation and fibrosis

Triggers

Asbestos: shipyards, construction, plumbing, insulation, brake linings

Silica: sandblasting, mining, foundries, stone countertops; coal: coal mining

Beryllium: aerospace and electronics manufacturing

Chain

Nodules coalesce progressive massive fibrosis restrictive lungs with a low diffusing capacity

Fibrosis cor pulmonale, most with berylliosis and silicosis

Insights

Latency runs 20 to 30 years, so a job left decades ago still counts

Pleural plaques alone mark exposure; they are benign and need no treatment

The lobes in one word: Lobe mnemonicUpper lobes: Silica, Beryllium, Coal. Asbestos is the one at the bases.

4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Pneumoconiosis with rheumatoid arthritis and lung nodulesCaplan syndromeCoal, silica or asbestos history

Pause point. The bait: a cancer question in an asbestos worker. Mesothelioma is the famous answer, but bronchogenic carcinoma is far more common, and smoking multiplies only the carcinoma.

Practice
  1. 62 yo M shipyard insulator with lower-lobe fibrosis and pleural plaques → Asbestosis
  2. 55 yo M sandblaster with upper-lobe nodules and eggshell-calcified hilar nodes → Silicosis
  3. 58 yo M coal miner with upper-lobe nodules and black sputum → Coal workers' pneumoconiosis
  4. 50 yo M aerospace machinist with noncaseating granulomas on biopsy → Berylliosis
  5. 45 yo F cotton mill worker with chest tightness worst on the first day back at work → Byssinosis
  6. 40 yo M pigeon breeder with fever and dyspnea 6 hours after exposure → Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
  7. 62 yo M with asbestos exposure, a pleural mass and an effusion → Mesothelioma
  8. 55 yo M sandblaster and never smoker with silicosis → Annual tuberculin skin test → silicosis raises tuberculosis risk
  9. 66 yo M, retired shipyard worker, asymptomatic, with calcified pleural plaques and normal lung parenchyma on imaging → No treatment → plaques alone mark exposure and are benign
  10. 62 yo M with decades of asbestos exposure who also smokes heavily → Bronchogenic carcinoma → smoking multiplies bronchogenic risk only, not mesothelioma
  11. 50 yo M aerospace machinist with progressive dyspnea and noncaseating granulomas on biopsy, now removed from exposure → Oral corticosteroids → berylliosis responds to steroids
Mnemonic and timing Asbestos comes from the roof but affects the base; silica and coal come from the ground but affect the top. Latency is typically 20–30 years, so exposure that ended decades ago still counts. Pleural plaques alone are a marker of exposure, benign, and need no treatment.
Transferable rule Answering a long stem in under 40 seconds means one cue was pattern-matched and the verification pass was skipped. This costs the most in occupational stems. The lobe distribution usually decides the diagnosis, and it comes at the end of the stem.
